name: Carvajal syndrome
aliases: woolly hair, keratoderma and cardiomyopathy syndrome

clinicalPearls: A triad of woolly hair, striate (often epidermolytic) palmoplantar keratoderma, and a cardiomyopathy
The cardiomyopathy is classically a dilated / left-dominant arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, contrasting with the right-dominant pattern of Naxos disease
Woolly hair and keratoderma are typically evident from infancy, preceding recognition of cardiac disease
Caused by recessive mutations in DSP encoding desmoplakin, a key desmosomal plaque protein
Life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia, heart failure and sudden cardiac death are the principal dangers
Any child with woolly hair and palmoplantar keratoderma warrants cardiac evaluation
Management centres on cardiological surveillance and heart-failure/arrhythmia care, with emollients/keratolytics for the skin
reference.pathophysiology: Carvajal syndrome is usually an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in DSP, which encodes desmoplakin, an obligate component of the desmosomal plaque that anchors intermediate filaments to the cell membrane. Desmosomes provide mechanical coupling between cells, and desmoplakin dysfunction weakens cell-cell adhesion in tissues subject to mechanical stress. In the epidermis this produces the keratoderma and, with hair-shaft involvement, woolly hair; in the myocardium impaired desmosomal integrity leads to myocyte detachment, fibrofatty replacement and an arrhythmogenic, dilated (frequently left-ventricular predominant) cardiomyopathy that predisposes to arrhythmia and sudden death.
additionalDifferentials: Naxos disease (JUP/plakoglobin mutation, right-dominant arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy)
Other arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathies without cutaneous features
Woolly hair naevus or isolated woolly hair
Striate palmoplantar keratoderma of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Electrocardiography and Holter monitoring for arrhythmia
Echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging to characterise the cardiomyopathy and fibrofatty change
Hair microscopy demonstrating woolly hair-shaft abnormalities
Skin biopsy of keratoderma (may show epidermolytic change)
Family cardiac screening and genetic counselling
redFlags: Palpitations, syncope or documented ventricular arrhythmia
Symptoms or signs of heart failure
Family history of premature sudden cardiac death
reference.prognosis: The cutaneous and hair features are benign, but prognosis is dictated by the cardiomyopathy, which can cause heart failure, life-threatening arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death, sometimes in childhood or adolescence. Early cardiac surveillance and intervention substantially influence outcome.
pitfalls: Regarding woolly hair and keratoderma as a purely cosmetic dermatological problem and omitting cardiac assessment
Assuming the right-dominant Naxos pattern when Carvajal is typically left-dominant/dilated
Delaying cardiological referral until cardiac symptoms appear
Not screening at-risk family members for arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy
management: Heart-failure therapy for the dilated cardiomyopathy with ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists and diuretics
Arrhythmia management with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for those at high risk of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death
Restriction from competitive and high-intensity exercise to reduce arrhythmic risk
Topical treatment of the palmoplantar keratoderma with emollients and keratolytic agents
Regular cardiac surveillance with electrocardiography, Holter monitoring and imaging, given progression of the cardiomyopathy
Consideration of cardiac transplantation for end-stage heart failure
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive DSP disease, with cardiac screening of relatives
